```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
library(skimr)
library(scales)
library(ggvenn)
library(broom)
conflicted::conflict_prefer("select", "dplyr")
conflicted::conflict_prefer("filter", "dplyr")
```

# Load in the messy data files provided in the repository.

If you have downloaded the files to your computer, update the path below to point to the correct storage location.

# Participants Table
```{r}
# Read the participant data table into your R environemnt. Note that thetable is a tab-delimited .txt file and not comma-delimited .csv and it must be read with read_tsv() to parse correctly as one of the columns and several of the data values contain commas that create incorrect parsing.
raw_participants <- read_tsv("messy_participants.txt", show_col_types = TRUE)
raw_participants_as_csv <- read_csv("messy_participants.txt", show_col_types = TRUE)

View(raw_participants)
View(raw_participants_as_csv)

#If you are working in Positron, you can also use the sidebar of the file viewer to get some of this information
skim(raw_participants)
```

Note several things we will want to notice and fix with this table.
1. The column names contain some special characters and units that will make them difficult to work with in R. We will want to clean these up.
2. The Leukocyte count column is being read as a string (characters) rather than numeric because the value 7.1 x10^9/L and the text word "missing" are not numbers. Values in this column should be coerced to numeric and "missing" represented as NA.
3. Similarly, blood pressure, height, weight, and date columns are being read as strings due to the presence of units and mixed formatting.
4. The date column is inconsistently formatted and needs to be standardized if we want to use it as a date in any visualizations or analyses.
5. There is a missing value for participant P04's age. If we review the "Notes" column, we can see that the investigator meant to fill that in from other sources but has not done so. This value should be added to the data sheet if it is available, or can be left as NA for truly missing. Do not fill a missing value with a placeholder like "unknown", "missing", or a dummy value.
6. There are values in Leukocyte count ("missing" and "999") that *should be* represented as NA so that the code and downstream analysis recognizes these as missing values.

```{r}
# Lets begin by tidying the column names which will make future code easier to write and read. We will use the convenient janitor::clean_names() function to do this. This will convert all column names to lowercase, replace spaces and special characters with underscores, and remove units from the column names. This way we can refer to the columns with simple names like "age_years" instead of "Age (years)" which would require backticks in R code.
participants <- raw_participants %>% 
  clean_names()
```

For those new to R, renaming the object from `raw_participants` to `participants` is creating a new object in the R environment that contains the same data but with cleaned column names. This is a common practice in data cleaning workflows to keep the original raw data separate and unmodified, while creating new objects as we process to analysis-ready versions. This way, if we make a mistake in the cleaning process, we can always go back to the original raw data that we'd loaded. Note as well that an R object will not overwrite the actual raw .csv or .txt file on your computer -- these objects only exist in your R environment. The raw files on your computer will remain unchanged unless/until you explicitly write over them with a function like `write_csv()`.

## Look at the participants data:

### Age at enrollment
Lets plot a histogram to see distribution of ages. Note that P04 is missing age data and will be excluded from this plot with a warning. But everything else looks as expected.
```{r}
# Lets plot a histogram to see distribution of ages. Note that P04 is missing age data and will be excluded from this plot with a warning.
ggplot(participants, aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of participants",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Note that if we do a math function on this data without telling the code to ignore NA values we can get an NA result for the calculation. This is intended to warn you - the user - that there are undefined values in that column and prevent a *silent* failure that could be misleading by requiring you to intentionally choose that you are OK to ignore missing.
median(participants$age_years)

#Adding the na.rm=TRUE argument tells the code you are comfortable ignoring the NA values, and the median should be calculated only on the available data.
median(participants$age_years, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Sex
Distribution by sex, using a bar chart
```{r}
participants %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = "Participants", fill = sex_m_f)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", width = 0.6, color = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "Participant Sex Distribution (100% Stacked)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percent",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# This reinforces that the code sees each different text string as a different category, despite the distinction between "M", "Male", and "MALE" being entirely meaningless and obviously identical to a human reader. We will want to standardize these values to a consistent text format.
# There are many ways this can be done, but here we'll use some stringr functions to recode the values by recognizing common patterns and dismissing all variations on case to lowercase. Because we have no interest in preserving the original text values, we will simply overwrite the column based on this formula. If we want to review the original values, we can look back at the raw_participants object which is unchanged.
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(sex_m_f = case_when(
    str_to_lower(sex_m_f) %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female",
    str_to_lower(sex_m_f) %in% c("m", "male")   ~ "Male",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

#Much better
participants %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = "Participants", fill = sex_m_f)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", width = 0.6, color = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "Participant Sex Distribution (100% Stacked)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percent",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


### Phenotypes

This column is very complex. A few things to note when you look at it:
1. There is more than one thing described, as inforamtion about the affected status (healthy volunteer versus clinically described participants) are blended into the same column. If we want to treat healthy volunteers differently from affected participants, we will want to separate those concepts into two columns.
2. There are multiple phenotypes listed in some cells, but they are delimited inconsistently with semicolons, pipes, and commas. If we simply want to use these as descriptive, we may be ok to leave those as they are. But if we want the code to recognize this as a list of multiple values rather than a single value of (phenotype1; phenotype2; phenotype3), we will want to split these into multiple rows or conver the column to a list columns.
3. There may be a particular phenotype of interest that we want to use as a variable in the analysis. This conceptual variable may be an umbrella term that covers more than one of the more detailed terms attributed to the participant. For example, if we want to compare participants with infections to those without, or count participants with documented evidence for intellectual disability.

```{r}
# Create a new column "affected" that is derived from the phenotype column. If the phenotype contains the word "healthy", then Affected == "Healthy". If the phenotype contains any other value, then affected status is "Affected". 
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(affected = if_else(
    str_to_lower(phenotype) == "healthy volunteer", "Healthy", "Affected"
  ))

#We may then want to use logic to remove the "Healthy volunteer" from the phenotype column, while preserving the other phenotypes.
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(phenotype = case_when(
    affected == "Healthy" ~ NA_character_,
    TRUE ~ phenotype
  ))
```

Now, we are interested in creating a variable (column) that flags any participants who have intellectual disability. We will use our biomedical understanding to choose terms that we know are associated with this trait, and str_detect() which can look for partial matches, meaning we don't need to split the phenotypes before running this code.
```{r}
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(intellectual_disability = case_when(
    str_detect(str_to_lower(phenotype), "intellectual disability|developmental delay|intell|cognitive") ~ TRUE,
    .default = FALSE))

# Count how many participants have intellectual disability according to this flag.
participants %>%
  group_by(intellectual_disability) %>%
  summarize(n=n_distinct(participant_id))

```

### Leukocyte Count

We need to convert this to numeric and represent the missing/dummy values as NA. 
```{r}
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(leukocyte_count = str_remove(leukocyte_count, "\\s*x10\\^9/L"),
         leukocyte_count = na_if(leukocyte_count, "missing"),
         leukocyte_count = na_if(leukocyte_count, "999"),
         leukocyte_count = as.numeric(leukocyte_count))

#Distribution across the cohort
ggplot(participants, aes(x = leukocyte_count)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Leukocyte count distribution",
       x = "Leukocytes", y = "#Participants") +
  theme_minimal()

#Value for each particpant, graphically. We can see that largely values lie within the normal range with two missing participants and a severe outlier in P04 that is actually expected for this individual.
ggplot(participants, aes(x = participant_id, y = leukocyte_count)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Leukocyte count by participant",
       x = "Participant ID", y = "Leukocytes") +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Blood Pressure

Blood pressure here is being read as a string because of the "\" character that is splitting the systolic and diastolic values. We will want to split this into two separate columns for systolic and diastolic blood pressure and convert those to numeric. 
```{r}
participants <- participants %>%
  separate(
    blood_pressure_mm_hg,
    into = c("bp_systolic", "bp_diastolic"),
    sep = "\\s*\\/\\s*"
  )
```


Note that representing P08 as N/A actually splits the value as well, but into "N" and "A", and keeps the columns as character. We want to get rid of this. Coercing to convert the column to numeric blanks out these values and gives us a user warning that it has introduced NAs with this conversion. In this case - exactly what we wanted to happen so we move on. But if you did not expect any non-numeric values in the column, this warning should make you look back at the data and make sure you have not introduced errors or dropped data.
```{r}
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(bp_systolic = as.numeric(bp_systolic),
         bp_diastolic = as.numeric(bp_diastolic))
```

### Height
```{r}
#As in previous examples, we want to remove the units from this cell and have these recognized as numbers
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(height_cm = as.numeric(str_remove(height, "\\s*cm"))) %>%
  select(-height)
```

```{r}
# Plot the distribution. Here, we see a clear outlier and we want to review that for plausibility.
participants %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = height_cm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Height distribution of participants",
       x = "Height (cm)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Find out who has a height less than 100cm. Here, we see that individual P03 is the outlier, and is also 3years old, thus the short stature is plausible.
participants %>%
  filter(height_cm < 100) %>%
  dplyr::select(participant_id, age_years, height_cm)
```

### Weight

There are several data entry errors embedded in this column. 
```{r}
# Lets try to evaluate the range first. What we actually see is an alphabetic/alphanumeric sorting where starts with 1 is the minimum and starts with 9 is the maximum. This is not what we'd wanted to see.
min(participants$weight)
max(participants$weight)

# This time, let's split the units from the numeric values first rather than just dropping them as we'd done before. We'll send all numbers to the value "weight_num" and all letters to the column "unit" to take a look. 
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(
    weight_num = parse_number(weight),
    unit = str_extract(weight, "[[:alpha:]]+") %>% str_to_lower()
  )

# Here, we see two clear things that need addressing. First, we have mixed units (lb and kg) that need to be reviewed and standardized. Second, we have a clear outlier with weight of 2kg which needs to be investigated as a possible data entry error.
participants %>%
  dplyr::select(weight, weight_num, unit) %>%
  arrange(desc(weight_num))

# After we review notes and are confident that the "lbs" value is truly recorded in pounds and needs conversion (vs a typo when writing units into the table), we can mathematically do that here.
participants<-participants %>%
  mutate(weight_kg = case_when(
    unit == "lbs" ~ weight_num / 2.205,
    TRUE ~ weight_num
  ))

# Check our conversion success
participants %>%
  dplyr::select(participant_id, weight, weight_num, unit, weight_kg) %>%
  arrange(desc(weight_kg))

# Now drop the other columns to avoid future confusion, keeping only the weight in kg as a cleaned variable for future analysis.
participants <- participants %>%
  select(-weight, -weight_num, -unit)

# Plot the distribution of weight in kg.
participants %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weight_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Weight distribution of participants",
       x = "Weight (kg)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r}
# The participant with recorded weight of 2kg is is clearly a data entry error, even for a 3yr old. If possible, we will want to return to any original source notes to see if the value can be corrected to a true value, but barring that, we will want to blank it out as missing, rather than allowing the error to enter our analysis. In this example, the true value is found in notes as 24kg. This can be corrected on the original data sheet, but we'll demonstrate how to do it here as well.

# For any weight value less than 5kg, replace with 24kg. We could also be exact and use for weight_kg == 2 then 24.
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(weight_kg = case_when(
    weight_kg < 5 ~ 24, # based on review of notes
    .default = weight_kg
  ))

participants %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weight_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 120)) +
  labs(title = "Weight of participants",
       x = "Weight (kg)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Dates

The recorded dates appear to be entered pretty freely and inconsistently. We even have a date that appears to have been auto-converted to an Excel serial number.
```{r}
unique(participants$date_of_enrollment)
```

LLMs can create a variety of custom scripts capable of parsing dates, relying on the janitor::convert_to_date or lubridate::parse_date_time functions which are designed to recognize dates specifically and standardize their representations. 
```{r}
# This is a complex custom function, but if you're working with an LLM code assistant - you don't need to write it, you just need to review the input and output as matching, and make sure the LLM is accurately parsing all the variety properly. While you can overwrite the column, here we'll create a second column (date_of_enrollment_std) that allows manual comparison with the input.
participants <- participants %>%
  mutate(
    date_of_enrollment_std = janitor::convert_to_date(
      date_of_enrollment,
      character_fun = \(x) {
        x <- stringr::str_squish(x)

        is_excel_num <- stringr::str_detect(x, "^\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$")

        out <- rep(as.Date(NA), length(x))

        # Excel serial date (origin handles Excel's date system)
        out[is_excel_num] <- as.Date(as.numeric(x[is_excel_num]), origin = "1899-12-30")

        # Character dates like 3/14/21 or June 7 2021
        out[!is_excel_num] <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
          x[!is_excel_num],
          orders = c("mdy", "B d Y", "b d Y")
        ) |>
          as.Date()

        out
      }
    )
  )

participants %>%
  select(participant_id, date_of_enrollment, date_of_enrollment_std)
```

### Reorganize your table to bring columns you want to see together, together
```{r}
participants <- participants %>%
  select(participant_id, affected, date_of_enrollment_std, age_years, sex_m_f, height_cm, weight_kg, everything())
```

### Admire your work

Notice which columns are now properly represented as numeric or dates, check the missing fraction as expected, see minimums, maximums, completion rate summaries, etc. You're ready to go.
```{r}
skim(participants)
```

# Variants Table

Read in the data about which participants carry which variants, and some annotation information about them
```{r}
raw_variants <- read_tsv("messy_variants.txt", show_col_types = TRUE)

skim(raw_variants)
View(raw_variants)
```

Plenty of data cleanup required here too. As we walked through it before, we'll combine several steps in our first pass.

```{r}
variants<-raw_variants %>%
  clean_names() %>%

# create a duplicate of the genomic coordinates column so we can work with it as an ID (chr-pos-ref-alt) and/or as chromosomal and numeric positional data. 
  mutate(genomic_position = genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt) %>%

# split one of the duplicates into chrom, pos, ref and alt columns
  separate(
    genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt,
    into = c("chrom", "pos", "ref", "alt"),
    sep = "-",
    extra = "merge"
  ) %>%

# Convert the position column to numeric
  mutate(pos = as.integer(pos)) %>%

# Convert variant type to title case for standardization and readability
  mutate(variant_type = str_to_title(variant_type)) %>%

# Separate the hgvsc and hgvsp to individual columns based on the / delimiter. 
  separate(
    hgvs_hgv_sc_hgv_sp,
    into = c("hgvsc", "hgvsp"),
    sep = "\\s*/\\s*"
  ) %>%

# The simple separation leaves some leading and trailing whitespaces. We want to get rid of those as code treats them as characters that are part of the value. The str_trim() function is designed to do just that. 
# In addition, variants affecting non-coding sequences seem to have hgvsp represented with a dot "." to represent not applicable. We would like to convert that to NA, and so if trimming the leading and trailing spaces leaves us with just a dot - na_if() does this for us.
  mutate(hgvsp = na_if(str_trim(hgvsp), "."))
```

```{r}
# Let's find any values that are blank for hgvsp
variants %>%
  filter(is.na(hgvsp)) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_zygosity, variant_type, hgvsc, hgvsp, chrom, pos)
```

Above, we could see that there are three variant rows where no hgvsp is provided. Two of these are expected as the variant lands in an non-coding region and thus does not have a protein coding change. The third reveals a more complex situation. This participant has an extra copy of chromosome 21 which is definitely information we want; however the gene and variant information about that is not being well-represented in the table. We need to make a decision about how we want to capture it.

Decision: add variant type as "chromosome_duplication", leave hgvsc and hgvsp blank, and document the chrom, pos, ref, and alt in a custom fashion with "N" (for normal) and "SV" (for copy number 3) ref/alt configuration. These particular choices are entirely arbitrary for this purpose and do not reflect best practices in genomics for representation of copy number variants. 

Our goal in doing this is so that if/when we want to count the number of unique variants by looking at unique values in the chrom-pos-ref-alt columns, this variant will actually be counted as a variant and not left uncounted as an NA/missing or counted as a non-distinct/duplicate value if more than one NA is present in the table.

```{r}
# Participants with at least one variant in the table. 
# The function n_distinct() does count NA as a unique value even though that may not be intuitive behaviour to an analyst, so we want to use sum(!is.na(genomic_position)) to count only non-missing variants.
variants %>%
  group_by(participant) %>%
  summarize(n_variants = sum(!is.na(genomic_position)))

# Fill in the custom information we decided above for documenting trisomy into this table. This is writing the missing information into our R object.
variants<-variants %>%
  mutate(
    variant_type = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "trisomy 21") ~ "chromosome_duplication",
      TRUE ~ variant_type
    ),
    chrom = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "trisomy 21") ~ "chr21",
      TRUE ~ chrom
    ),
    ref = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "trisomy 21") ~ "N",
      TRUE ~ ref
    ),
    alt = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "trisomy 21") ~ "SV",
      TRUE ~ alt
    ),
    genomic_position = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "trisomy 21") ~ "chr21-CN3",
      TRUE ~ genomic_position
    )
  )

# We can now see that participant P07 has two distinct, non-NA variants accounted for. Just what we wanted.
variants %>%
  group_by(participant) %>%
  summarize(n_variants = sum(!is.na(genomic_position)))
```

### The gene and zygosity information is blended in one column. After taking a look at the table, we see we need to do a few operations here. 

```{r}
# First, we want to separate 
variants <- variants %>%

# Strip off leading and trailing whitespace
  mutate(
    gene_zygosity = str_squish(gene_zygosity),

# Since we noticed the unnecessary dash in MECP2 (not part of the formal gene name per HGNC nomenclature), let's remove that too. This script replaces every "-" with nothing instead "". More complex functions would be possible but are not necessary in this dataset
    gene_zygosity = str_replace_all(gene_zygosity, regex("-", ignore_case = TRUE), ""),

# We will try to extract gene names from their current representation by taking the leading alphanumeric characters before the first space or parenthesis, and converting to uppercase for standardization. Zygosity will be captured by detecting strings that match hemi, hom, or het patterns, ignoring case. Because we bring the knowledge that germline PTEN as a secondary finding must be heterozyous, we'll match that into the pattern, though it is best practice to review the raw data.
   gene = gene_zygosity %>%
      str_extract("^[A-Za-z0-9]+") %>%
      str_to_upper(),
    zygosity = case_when(
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "hem") ~ "Hemizygous",
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "hom") ~ "Homozygous",
      str_detect(gene_zygosity, "het|secondary") ~ "Heterozygous",
      .default = NA_character_
      )
    )

# See how we did? Looks pretty good though there remains some missing data - it was missing in the input
variants %>%
  select(gene_zygosity, gene, zygosity) %>%
  arrange(gene)
```

We know that the information on gene zygosity must exist for all the variants, and it is missing simply because it was not recorded. So this calls for returning to source documents to fill in the missing information. We will assume source documentation reveals that the two short variants with missing zygosity are actually heterozygous.
```{r}
variants <- variants %>%
  mutate(zygosity = case_when(
    gene == "TRISOMY" ~ "CN3",
    is.na(zygosity) ~ "Heterozygous",
    TRUE ~ zygosity
  ))

variants %>%
  select(gene_zygosity, gene, zygosity) %>%
  arrange(gene)

# Drop the gene_zygosity column now that we have extracted the information we wanted from it into separate columns.
variants <- variants %>%
  select(-gene_zygosity)
```

## Now we look at the data to get familiar with it
```{r}
# How many unique variants do we have?
n_distinct(variants$genomic_position)

# How many participants are on this table with a variant described?
n_distinct(variants$participant)

# What types of variants are present in this table?
count(variants, variant_type)

# Which genes are present with annotated variants, and what kinds? Who carries them?
variants %>%
  group_by(gene) %>%
  summarize(
    nVariants=n_distinct(genomic_position),
    nParticipants=n_distinct(participant),
    variant_types = paste(unique(variant_type), collapse = "; "),
    carriers = paste(unique(participant), collapse = "; ")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(nParticipants))
```

# Annotations Table.

Load in the annotations table from file
```{r}
raw_annotations <- read_csv("messy_annotations.csv", show_col_types = TRUE)

skim(raw_annotations)
View(raw_annotations)
```

Looking at the data we see:
1. A funny looking character "\n17-40554783-T-C" that is a hidden newline. This will create problems for parsing, joining and printing the table, and it's not part of the intended value. We want to get rid of it.
2. The gene HBB has a parenthetical (HbS) next to it as this is the variant responsible for sickle cell trait/disease and that nomenclature may be very familiar to a researcher. However, if we want to join material based on gene name, "HBB" and "HBB (HbS)" will not be recognized as the same gene.
3. The allele frequency needs to be coerced to numeric if we want to use frequency-based filtering for the minor allele frequency. Also we want to ensure that a value of NA (which we have confirmed as "variant not seen in gnomAD") is treated as a true zero frequency showing that it is ultrarare, rather than a variant with no information. 
4. Variant prediction scores from SpliceAI, AlphaMissense, and REVEL also need to be converted to numeric. For SpliceAI and REVEL, there are multiple values separated by "&" that represent scores for different isoforms. We decide to take the maximum across those isoforms to get a single value for each variant.


```{r}
# Clean column names and remove all hidden characters from the table
annotations <- raw_annotations %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      \(x) x %>%
        str_replace_all("\u00A0", " ") %>%                     # non-breaking spaces
        str_replace_all("[\u200B-\u200D\uFEFF]", "") %>%       # zero-width chars
        str_replace_all("[[:cntrl:]]+", " ") %>%               # tabs/newlines/control chars
        str_squish()                                           # trim + collapse internal whitespace
    )
  )

# Separate the gene column again using the first space, keeping only the gene name and discarding everything after
annotations <- annotations %>%
  separate_wider_delim(cols = gene, delim = " ", names = c("gene", NA), too_few = "align_start")
```

### Move onto allele frequency
```{r}
#Look for any NA/empty values
annotations %>%
  filter(is.na(af_gnom_ad)) %>%
  select(gene, af_gnom_ad)

# Creating a new intermediate data frame, we update input NA to zero and coerce to numeric. 
a<-annotations %>%
  mutate(af_gnom_ad = case_when(
    is.na(af_gnom_ad) ~ 0,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(af_gnom_ad)
  ))

# However, we can see that coercing to numeric has turned the value `4.968e-6 into an new NA as the leading tick mark made it recognized as a string/text value (a warning was printed). Other small numbers that are merely in scientific notation are properly recongized as numeric. This is not acceptable. If we were to leave this in and apply a frequency filter to retain or flag any variants that are below (or above) a certain frequency, this variant would be dropped from the analysis entirely due to the NA value (indeterminate frequency). This can create silent errors.
a %>%
  filter(is.na(af_gnom_ad)) %>%
  select(gene, af_gnom_ad)

# Instruct the code to remove the leading tick mark prior to converting values to numeric.
annotations<-annotations %>%
  mutate(af_gnom_ad = case_when(
    is.na(af_gnom_ad) ~ 0,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(str_replace(af_gnom_ad, "^`", ""))
  ))

# Now we can see zero remaining NA values in this column
annotations %>% 
  filter(is.na(af_gnom_ad)) %>%
  select(gene, af_gnom_ad)
```

```{r}
# Plot distribution of allele frequencies. We can see that two variants have MAF of 0 (absent from gnomAD), most variants are ultrarare with in gnomAD, and a few have low but non-zero frequencies. One variant stands out as common with a MAF exceeding 50%. Depending on our goals, this variant may need to be reviewed.
ggplot(annotations, aes(x = af_gnom_ad)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.001, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Allele frequency distribution in gnomAD",
       x = "Allele Frequency", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() 

min(annotations$af_gnom_ad)
max(annotations$af_gnom_ad)

annotations %>%
  filter(af_gnom_ad > 0.1) %>%
  select(gene, genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt, clinvar, af_gnom_ad)
```

### Clinvar
```{r}
# Review values in the clinvar column
unique(annotations$clinvar)

# Lets consolidate into a simplified set of categories. It may be beneficial to review the evidence on ClinVar before accepting an assertion, and/or to understand what may be meant by "conflicting interpretations of pathogenicity".
# In order to avoid having the code recognize "Conflicting interpretations of <b>pathogenic</b>ity" as "Pathogenic" due to the presence of the word "pathogenic", we will use case_when() which is an ordered function. This checks for the condition "Conflicting" before "Pathogenic" to ensure only one simplified value is retained for each variant. 
# Because capitalization varies, we will ensure str_detect() ignores case
annotations <- annotations %>%
  mutate(clinvar_simple = case_when(
    str_detect(clinvar, regex("Conflicting", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Conflicting",
    str_detect(clinvar, regex("Pathogenic", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "PLP",
    str_detect(clinvar, regex("Benign", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "BLB",
    str_detect(clinvar, regex("Uncertain", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "VUS",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

annotations %>%
  group_by(clinvar_simple, clinvar) %>%
  summarize(n = n_distinct(genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt))
```

### Bioinformatics predictions

There are several nuances to the values in the bioinformatics predictions. Certain variant types are not scored by certain algorithms and thus have NA values that are expected and appropriate. For example, AlphaMissense and REVEL only provides scores for missense variants. We want to be sure to recognize these as appropriately missing based on the variant type, rather than as errors or as zero values.

We can also notice that there are a few rows where isoform-specific scores are provided with an "&" delimiter. We will take the maximum score across isoforms to get a single value for each variant, but other approaches could be taken depending on the goals of the analysis.

```{r}
# Look at the distribution of SpliceAI scores. We can see that most variants have a score of zero, but a few have higher scores that may be of interest. We also see that the maximum score across isoforms is being properly captured for those with multiple isoform scores.
# First, we'll look just at what happens if we plot the raw values that are coercible to numeric without additional parsing. 
ggplot(annotations %>% mutate(splice_ai = as.numeric(splice_ai)), aes(x = splice_ai)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "SpliceAI score distribution",
       x = "Max SpliceAI Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Do the same for AlphaMissense scores. 
ggplot(annotations %>% mutate(alpha_missense_score = as.numeric(alpha_missense_score)), aes(x = alpha_missense_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "AlphaMissense score distribution",
       x = "AlphaMissense Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Repeat for REVEL scores
ggplot(annotations %>% mutate(revel = as.numeric(revel)), aes(x = revel)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "REVEL score distribution",
       x = "REVEL Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# We might reasonably expect that AlphaMissense and REVEL scores may be correlated. Let's take a look. Our dataset is a bit too small to do this well, but a correlation does appear to be there.
ggplot(annotations %>% mutate(alpha_missense_score = as.numeric(alpha_missense_score), revel = as.numeric(revel)), aes(x = alpha_missense_score, y = revel)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "AlphaMissense vs REVEL scores",
       x = "AlphaMissense Score", y = "REVEL Score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Fix and preprocess the scores

Ensure that all values present are numeric and missing values are encoded with NA.

When doing complex parsing like this, it may be preferable to create a new object rather than overwriting the existing object. This allows you to make more mistakes and compare the actual outcome with your intention.
```{r}
annotations_processed <- annotations %>%
  mutate(
    splice_ai = case_when(
      str_detect(splice_ai, "&") ~ str_split(splice_ai, "&") %>% map_dbl(~ max(as.numeric(.x), na.rm = TRUE)),
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(splice_ai)
    ),
    alpha_missense_score = case_when(
      str_detect(alpha_missense_score, "&") ~ str_split(alpha_missense_score, "&") %>% map_dbl(~ max(as.numeric(.x), na.rm = TRUE)),
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(alpha_missense_score)
    ),
    revel = case_when(
      str_detect(revel, "&") ~ str_split(revel, "&") %>% map_dbl(~ max(as.numeric(.x), na.rm = TRUE)),
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(revel)
    )
  )

# We can notice that the REVEL score derived from .&. is -INF instead of NA. This makes sense, because there is no mathematical maximum between . and ., however we want to clean up our table and make that an NA for consistency. The pale -INF is a special value, not a character that reads "-INF", so we use a function appropriate for this.
annotations_processed <- annotations_processed %>%
  mutate(revel = if_else(is.infinite(revel), NA_real_, revel))
```

# Bring data together

Combining data tables is a common and very straightforward process when you are working computationally. 

If two tables have a common ID variable, you can use that directly. If the two tables have a variable representing a common ID but with different column names, or slightly different formatting, you can do some quick parsing to get those into alignment and then join.

## Join annotations to variants
```{r}
# How many unique variants in the variants table?
n_distinct(variants$genomic_position)

# How many unique variants in the annotations table?
n_distinct(annotations_processed$genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt)
```

Check overlap between the two tables. Both seem to have 16 variants, but are they the same 16?

```{r}
# How many variants are shared between the two tables based on the genomic position? This is a test query; not yet the join.
variants %>%
  inner_join(annotations_processed, by = c("genomic_position" = "genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt")) %>%
  nrow()

# We can see that this error is due to differently representing the same variant across the two tables. In the variants table we have the chr prefix and in the annotations table we do not. We can fix this with a quick parsing step to add the "chr" prefix to the chrom column in the annotations table so they should match up.
annotations_processed <- annotations_processed %>%
  mutate(genomic_position = paste0("chr", genomic_position_chr_pos_ref_alt))

variants %>%
  inner_join(annotations_processed, by = c("genomic_position" = "genomic_position")) %>%
  nrow()
```

```{r}
# Alternatively, we can review this with a Venn diagram.
table_variants_list <- list(
  variants = unique(variants$genomic_position),
  annotations = unique(annotations_processed$genomic_position)
)
```

```{r}
ggvenn(table_variants_list, 
  show_elements = FALSE)

# We can show the element labels in a Venn diagram.
ggvenn(table_variants_list, 
  show_elements = TRUE,
  label_sep = "\n",
  set_name_size = 4,
  text_size = 3)
```

We can see that there is one mysterious variant in the annotations table that is not in the variants table.
```{r}
#Find the variant in the annotations table that is not in the variants table
annotations_processed %>%
  filter(!genomic_position %in% variants$genomic_position) %>%
  select(gene, genomic_position, clinvar, af_gnom_ad)

#Reciprocally, find the variant in the variants table that is not in the annotations table
variants %>%
  filter(!genomic_position %in% annotations_processed$genomic_position) %>%
  select(participant, gene, genomic_position)

```

The trisomy 21 doesn't have a detailed variants match on the variants table, as the data present is only for short variants. So we will not be matching those with a table join, and this is expected. The SHANK3 variant (annotation table only) is simply not present in the variants table. This would be a moment to look back at notes, but may simply be that it was not observed in the set of participants that were considered for this analysis and that's how we'll treat it.

Bring all three tables together with full joins. Because we've carefully cleaned each table in advance, this process will go smoothly based on genomic position for variant information and participant ID for participant information. If we had not 
```{r}
# Left join the variants and annotation tables. We are only interested in bringing in annotations for the variants that were observed in our patients. This will exclude the SHANK3 variant that did not overlap
variants_annotations <- variants %>%
  left_join(annotations_processed, by = c("genomic_position" = "genomic_position", "gene" = "gene"))

skim(variants_annotations)

# Full join the variants_annotations table with the participants table.
variants_annotations_participants <- variants_annotations %>%
  full_join(participants, by = c("participant" = "participant_id"))

skim(variants_annotations_participants)
```

## Analysis

Describe the cohort
```{r}
# How many participants present?
n_distinct(variants_annotations_participants$participant)

# How many participants have at least one variant described?
n_distinct(variants_annotations_participants$participant[!is.na(variants_annotations_participants$genomic_position)])

# How many genes, and how many variants/gene
variants_annotations_participants %>%
  group_by(gene) %>%
  summarize(
    nVariants=n_distinct(genomic_position),
    variant_types = paste(unique(variant_type), collapse = ", "),
    nParticipants=n_distinct(participant)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(nParticipants))
```

# Filter to variants that are putatively functional
```{r}
variants_annotations_participants<-variants_annotations_participants %>%
  mutate(
    putatively_functional = case_when(
      clinvar_simple == "PLP" ~ TRUE,
      variant_type %in% c("Frameshift", "Stop_gain", "chromosome_duplication", "Splice Donor", "Splice Acceptor") ~ TRUE,
      splice_ai > 0.5 ~ TRUE,
      variant_type == "Missense" & (alpha_missense_score > 0.5 | revel > 0.5) ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )

# Number of participants with at least one putatively functional variant
variants_annotations_participants %>%
  group_by(putatively_functional) %>%
  summarize(n = n_distinct(participant))

# Predicted functional and not prioritized variants per participant
variants_annotations_participants %>%
  group_by(participant) %>%
  summarize(
    n_putatively_functional = sum(putatively_functional, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_not_prioritized = sum(!putatively_functional & !is.na(putatively_functional))
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_putatively_functional), desc(n_not_prioritized))
```

```{r}
# In this cohort, are putatively functional variants more likely to be found in participants with intellectual disability?
variants_annotations_participants %>%
  group_by(participant, intellectual_disability) %>%
  summarize(n_putatively_functional = sum(putatively_functional, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(intellectual_disability) %>%
  summarize(mean_putatively_functional = mean(n_putatively_functional))
```

In this cohort, are putatively functional variants more likely to be found in younger participants?
```{r}
# Because we know (and can describe) that the probability of a participant carrying a putatively functional variant is categorical (TRUE/FALSE), we want to use a logistic regression or a beta binomial test with age as the predictor.

# Create a processed data frame for each participant that has a single row/participant and documents their enrollment age as well as TRUE/FALSE for whether they have at least one putatively functional variant present.
age_analysis_df <- variants_annotations_participants %>%
  summarize(
    age_years = dplyr::first(age_years),
    any_functional = any(putatively_functional %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_functional = sum(putatively_functional %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = participant
  )

# Fit a logistic regression with age as the predictor (x) and detection of a putatively functional variant as the outcome (y). We use a binomial family to specify that the outcome is categorical (T/F or 1/0) rather than continuous.
logit_fit <- glm(
  any_functional ~ age_years,
  data = age_analysis_df,
  family = binomial()
)

logit_fit
```

In fitting the logistic regression, we see that the individual with missing age was necessarily dropped from the analysis as uninformative.

Prompting the LLM to describe the model output further if you are not familiar with it can be helpful to understand the results and how to interpret them. 

In this case, the coefficient for age_years is 0.00339, aka, near zero. This coefficient can be interpreted that with each additional year of age, the log-odds of having at least one putatively functional variant goes down by an nearly neglible amount. We can make this more interpretable, we can make this more interpretable by exponentiating the coefficients to get odds ratios, though this is simply making the same information in a more familiar way.

```{r}
logit_or <- tidy(
  logit_fit,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  exponentiate = TRUE
)

logit_or

# Similarly, this can be done manually as follows, revealing an odds ratio of 1.003 for every additional year of age.
coef(logit_fit) %>%
  exp()
```
